title: Express Basics
summary: Install Express 5, create an app, define routes with parameters and query strings, use the response helpers and serve static files, all in a few lines of code.
introduction: Express is the most widely used web framework for Node. It does not replace `node:http`; it wraps it, so the server you built by hand in the previous lesson becomes a handful of readable method calls: `app.get` for a route, `res.json` for a JSON reply, `req.params` for the pieces of a URL. This lesson covers Express 5, the version `npm install express` gives you today, and builds the first routes of the bookshelf API you will extend over the next three lessons.
learningObjectives: Create an Express app and define GET routes that return text and JSON
Read route parameters and query strings from the request
Choose the right response helper and serve static files

blocks.text: The hand-written server needed a URL parser, an `if` chain for routing, a JSON helper and a body reader. Express provides all four, plus a **middleware** pipeline (next lesson) that lets you add logging, authentication and error handling without touching every route. It is deliberately small: no database layer, no template engine by default, no opinion about how you organise files. That is why it pairs well with learning Node itself; nothing is hidden.
If you followed the [npm lesson](/tutorials/nodejs/setup-npm), Express is already installed. Otherwise run `npm install express` inside your project; `npm ls express` confirms the version:

blocks.title: npm ls express (your minor version may be newer)
app.js

items: `express()` creates the application. `app` is also a request handler, so `app.listen(port)` is `createServer(app).listen(port)` from `node:http` under the hood.
`app.get(path, handler)` registers a handler for GET requests to that path. `app.post`, `app.put`, `app.patch` and `app.delete` work the same way.
`res.send` sets `Content-Type` from the value (`text/html` for strings, JSON for objects) and ends the response; `res.json` always sends JSON. Neither needs `res.end`.
Express responds to unknown paths on its own with a `404` page containing `Cannot GET /missing`, so there is no hanging request for a typo in the URL.

blocks.text: A segment that starts with a colon is a **route parameter**: `/greet/:name` matches `/greet/Ada` and puts `'Ada'` in `req.params.name`. Anything after `?` in the URL is parsed into `req.query`. Both always contain strings.

blocks.title: greet.js
Parameters are strings
blocks.text: `req.params.id` for `/books/2` is the string `'2'`, so `books.find((b) => b.id === req.params.id)` never matches a numeric id and your route returns 404 for every book. Convert with `Number(req.params.id)` first, and check for `NaN` when the input comes from users. The same applies to `req.query.page`.

rows: A string as HTML, a Buffer as binary, an object or array as JSON; sets `Content-Length` and ends the response
JSON with `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`, even for strings and numbers
Sets the status code and returns `res`, so it chains: `res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' })`
Sets the status and sends its standard text as the body: `res.sendStatus(404)` sends `Not Found`
A `302` redirect (pass a code first for `301` or `303`)
Streams a file with the right `Content-Type`; the path must be absolute

blocks.title: A route that uses several helpers

blocks.text: The `return` before `res.status(404)` is the same discipline as in the raw server: one response per request. Express does not stop your function after `res.json`, so without the `return` the code would try to send a second response and log `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`.

`express.static(folder)` serves every file under a folder as-is: `public/index.html` becomes `/`, `public/css/site.css` becomes `/css/site.css`, with correct content types and caching headers. blocks.title: Serving the public folder
Express 5 versus Express 4
blocks.text: Most Express 4 tutorials still work, with three differences worth knowing. Express 5 forwards errors from `async` handlers to your error middleware automatically; route patterns use `/files/*name` for wildcards and `/users{/:id}` for optional segments instead of the old `*` and `?` syntax; and `req.body` may be `undefined` until a body-parsing middleware runs. Express 5 needs Node 18 or newer, so Node 24 is fully supported.

questions.question: The route is `app.get('/books/:id', ...)` and the request is `/books/42?format=short`. Which expression evaluates to `'42'`?
questions.explanation: Named route segments land in req.params; the query string lands in req.query. Both hold strings.

questions.question: After `res.json(book)` you must call `res.end()` to finish the response.
questions.explanation: res.json, res.send, res.redirect and res.sendFile all end the response themselves; res.end is only needed when you write the body manually.
